summary: This unit teaches you to handle guests' money correctly and safely at a villa, hotel or resort cash point. You will learn to open a cash point with a float, take cash and give the right change, check notes, work out US dollar payments at the property's rate, take card, phone, voucher and room-charge payments, deal with voids, refunds and disputes, keep cash secure, and cash up and reconcile at the end of the shift.

blocks.p: Almost every guest pays for something before leaving: a room, a meal, a drink, a tour, a spa treatment. The person at the cash point is trusted with the property's money and with guests' card details. One mistake can cost the property money, upset a guest, or look like theft. That is why this unit is about **accuracy, honesty and security** as much as arithmetic.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who will work at a front desk, restaurant, bar, shop or tour desk. You will use a cash drawer, a point of sale (POS) system or calculator, and a card terminal.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks with TRAINING money: opening a cash point and taking cash, US dollar, card and room-charge payments; then cashing up and handling problem payments. Never use real money, real cards or real guest details in the practical.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In Jamaica, bills show prices in Jamaican dollars (JMD, written J$). Many resorts also accept US dollars at a rate the property sets each day. GCT (General Consumption Tax) is charged on most bills at the current rate. Never use a rate or a tax figure from memory: use the one the property gives you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Opening the cash point and the float

blocks.p: A **float** is a set amount of cash, in small notes and coins, put in the drawer at the start of a shift so that you can give change to the first guests. The same float amount is there at the start of every shift. At the end of the shift it is counted out and set aside, and what remains is that shift's **cash takings**.

head: Float should have
Why
rows: Plenty of small notes and coins
Early guests often pay with large notes; without small money you cannot give change.
You need the right mix to give change without running out of one value.
The exact amount agreed for your cash point
So the shift's takings can be worked out later.

flow: Wash your hands, check your uniform and name badge, arrive on time
Collect the float from the supervisor, who should have it ready in a sealed bag or box
Count it with the supervisor, note by note and coin by coin
If the count matches the float sheet, both of you sign. If it does not, tell the supervisor at once and do not sign until it is corrected or recorded
Place the notes in the drawer face up, sorted by value, and the coins in their own sections
Log in to the POS with your own user name; check the date, prices and printer
Check the card terminal is on, charged and connected; check spare till rolls, pens, a calculator, bill pads and receipts
Check you have the exchange rate for the day, the service charge rate and the list of any approved vouchers

blocks.p: **Why count it with the supervisor?** You become responsible for the money the moment it is in your hands. If the count is wrong and you did not check, any shortage will be blamed on you. Counting together and signing protects both of you.
**Why a signed float sheet?** It is the record that the float was correct at the start. Without it, nobody can prove what was in the drawer.

blocks.h: Why notes face up and sorted

ul: You can find the right note quickly and give change without hunting, so guests are not kept waiting.
You count change correctly, because the notes are together by value.
Mistakes are easier to see when the drawer is neat.

blocks.p: Every cashier uses their own POS user name and code. This means each sale, void and refund can be traced to the right person. Never share your login or let anyone else use your drawer. If you leave, **log off or lock the screen and lock the drawer**.

blocks.note: Count large amounts of cash in a secure place such as a back office, out of the public's view, never at the counter in front of guests. The same goes for counting the float, if the supervisor allows it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Cash is quick and costs the property no bank fee, but it is the hardest payment to control. Follow the same steps every time.

flow: Tell the guest the total clearly
Take the money and say the amount aloud: 'Out of five thousand dollars'
Check the note is genuine
Leave the note on top of the drawer, not inside it
Key the amount received into the POS, which shows the change due
Take the change from the drawer and count it back to the guest
Put the guest's note in the drawer and close it
Give the receipt, and thank the guest

blocks.p: **Why leave the note on top of the drawer?** If the guest says, 'I gave you a bigger note,' you can both see what was handed over. Once it is in the drawer, nobody can prove it.
The best way to give change is to **count up from the bill to the amount paid**, saying each step aloud. This is how shopkeepers did it before tills could work out change, and it catches mistakes.

blocks.note: Check by subtraction too: guest pays minus bill equals change. J$10,000 minus J$7,250 equals J$2,750. If the POS shows a different figure from your own check, stop and look again before giving change.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every payment gets a **receipt**. It is proof of payment for the guest and the property. It must show the date, the items, GCT and any service charge, the total, the amount paid and the change. If you take a payment by hand (for example when the POS is down), write the receipt clearly and record it for later entry.
A **counterfeit** note is a fake note made to look like real money. If you take one, the property loses that amount, so check notes, especially large ones.

head: Check
How
rows: Real notes feel firm and have raised print you can feel with your fingertip. A very smooth, waxy or thin feel is a warning.
Hold it up to the light. Look for the watermark, a security thread and fine detail in the print. Polymer notes have a clear window.
Tilt the note to see features that change colour or shine.
Compare it with a note you know is real, of the same value.
If the property has an ultraviolet lamp, use it as you were trained.

blocks.note: The security features differ between note values and series. Your Centre will give you a guide from the Bank of Jamaica; use it. Do not rely on one test only.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: If you think a note is counterfeit

ul: Stay calm and polite. Do not accuse the guest: they may not know.
Do not hand the note back and do not throw it away or hide it.
Say, 'Please excuse me while I check this,' and call your supervisor, as the property's procedure says.
The supervisor decides what happens, which may include asking for another payment and reporting it.
Write down what happened: time, amount, guest description and who you spoke to.

blocks.note: Never put a suspect note back in the drawer, and never try to pass it on as change. That is a crime, even if you did not make it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Foreign currency: paying a J$ bill in US$

blocks.p: Many guests carry US dollars. Some properties allow them to pay a J$ bill in US$ cash, at the property's own rate. If your cash point does not take US$, send the guest to the front desk or another licensed place; the bar may not offer exchange.

ul: Use **only the exchange rate the property gives you for the day**. Not the rate a guest quotes from a bank or from a phone app.
Tell the guest the rate and show the working on the POS or a calculator, so they can see it is fair.
Check US$ notes for damage and for counterfeits just as you do for J$ notes. Some properties refuse badly torn notes.
Give change in the currency the property's policy says, usually J$.
Keep J$ and US$ in separate sections of the drawer, and count them separately at the end.
On the receipt, show the amount in US$, the rate used and the J$ total.

blocks.note: These examples use a practice rate of J$155 = US$1. Your property's rate will differ and may change every day.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A guest pays a J$9,300 bill in US$. How much is that in US$?
J$ amount divided by the rate: 9,300 / 155 = 60
The guest gives US$100. What change in J$?
US$100 less US$60 = US$40 change; US$40 x 155 = 6,200
A guest wants to pay a J$3,875 bill in US$.
A guest gives US$50 for a J$6,200 bill. Change in J$?

blocks.p: To change **US$ into J$**, multiply by the rate. To change **J$ into US$**, divide by the rate. Always work the sum twice, or check it with a calculator.

blocks.note: If a guest asks you to change US$200 into J$ cash and your cash point does not offer exchange, do not do it from the drawer. Politely direct the guest to the front desk or another licensed place. Cash taken from your drawer will not match your POS sales and will look like a shortage.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Payment
What it is
Key points for the cashier
rows: Takes money straight from the cardholder's own bank account.
The bank lends the money; the cardholder pays the bank later.
May need a PIN or a signature; approved by the card company.
Paying by holding a card or phone near the terminal, without inserting it.
For small amounts without a PIN, up to the limit the bank sets; above it the terminal asks for a PIN.
Paying by phone through an app the property accepts.
Wait for a confirmation on the screen before the guest leaves.
The bill is added to the guest's room account (folio) and paid at check-out.
Check name and room number, and get a signature.
A ticket, often from a tour company or promotion, for a meal or service already paid for.
Check it is valid, not expired, and meant for this property.

flow: Key in the correct amount and check it with the guest
Hand the terminal to the guest, or take it to the table, so the card stays in sight
The guest inserts the card (chip), taps it, or swipes it, and keys in the PIN themselves
Look away while the PIN is keyed in
Wait for 'Approved' and an authorisation code
Give the guest their copy; keep the property's copy for cashing up
Never leave the card on the counter

ul: **Chip:** the small gold or silver square on a bank card. The terminal reads it when the card is inserted. It is more secure than the old magnetic stripe.

**PIN** (personal identification number): a secret code that only the cardholder should know and key in. **Never ask a guest to tell you their PIN**, never write one down, and never write down the full card number.
**Authorisation code:** the code from the bank that shows a card payment was approved. It prints on the slip.
The terminal may ask you to check the card's expiry date and the name. Follow the property's rules.
Card receipts show only the **last four digits** of the card number, to protect the cardholder from fraud.

blocks.p: 'Declined' means the bank did not approve the payment. There may be no money in the account, the limit has been reached, the card is blocked, or the PIN was wrong. Do not guess the reason, and do not say it aloud.

flow: Tell the guest quietly: 'The terminal is not accepting this card'
Offer to try again, in case the card was read wrongly
If it is still declined, ask politely for another way to pay
Never argue, accuse or call out the problem in front of others
Call your supervisor if the guest cannot pay or becomes upset

blocks.note: Never keep a guest's card away from them. If a guest leaves a card behind, hand it to your supervisor, log it, and keep it secure. Do not try to use it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A guest staying at the property can have food, drinks and services **charged to the room**. The charge goes on the guest's account, called the **folio**, which lists all their charges until they pay at check-out.

ul: Ask for the guest's name and room number, or key card, and check them against the records on the POS.
Check that the room is allowed to take charges. Some guests are cash-only or have a credit limit.
Ask the guest to check the bill and sign it, with name and room number printed clearly. The signature is proof the guest agreed.
Post the charge to the right room straight away, so it appears on the folio.
Day visitors, and guests of other rooms, cannot charge to a room that is not theirs.
Check the voucher is genuine, has not expired, is for this property and covers what the guest is ordering.
Check the guest's name against the voucher if it names one.
Take the voucher, mark it used and keep it with the day's records; a voucher cannot be used twice.
If the voucher does not cover everything (for example drinks), take payment for the extra.
If you are not sure it is valid, call the supervisor before the guest orders.

sections.title: The bill, GCT and service charge

head: Item on the bill
What it is
rows: Each thing the guest bought, at the menu or price list price.
The total of the items before tax and service charge.
General Consumption Tax: a tax on sales, charged at the current rate. The property collects it for the government.
A percentage added for service, at the rate in the property's policy. Ask the supervisor if you do not know it.

blocks.note: Never quote a GCT or service charge figure from memory. The rates are set by law and by property policy, and they can change. Use the rate the POS and the property use, and ask your supervisor if a guest asks something you cannot answer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: When a guest says the bill is wrong

flow: Listen without interrupting and do not argue
Check the bill with the guest, item by item
Explain any charges the guest does not understand
If you made a mistake, say so, apologise and call the supervisor to approve a correction
If the guest still disagrees, call the supervisor; do not change the bill on your own

ul: A guest who is unsure what the total includes should be helped: go through each item and charge with them.
Be polite and keep your voice low; bill problems should not be shouted across the room.
Record any correction with the supervisor's approval.

head: Term
What it is
Who approves
rows: Cancelling an item or a whole sale on the POS **before** the guest pays.
Usually a supervisor, using their own code.
Giving money back **after** the guest has paid.
Changing a wrong price or item on a bill.
Reducing the price or giving an item free.

blocks.p: **Why must they be approved and recorded?** Voids and refunds take money out of the day's sales. Someone dishonest could ring up a sale, take the cash, then void it to hide the theft. Approval and a record protect the property, and they protect you from being blamed.

flow: Tell your supervisor straight away when a mistake happens or a guest asks for a refund
The supervisor checks the reason and approves it on the POS
Do the void or refund and keep the voided slip
Write it in the void or refund log with the time, the amount, the reason and both signatures
Include it in the cash-up

ul: **Ring up every sale.** If a friend or a colleague asks you not to ring up their drinks, politely refuse. Giving free drinks or food is stealing from the property, and it can cost you your job.
Never take money from the drawer, even to 'borrow' it, and never put your own money in.
Never move money between shifts or between drawers to cover a shortage or an overage. It hides errors and possible theft.
If you find an overage (more cash than expected), report it. Do not keep it.

blocks.note: Report your own mistakes immediately. A mistake reported at once is treated as an error. A mistake hidden may be treated as theft.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Risk
What to do
rows: Keep the drawer closed between sales. Open it only for a sale. If you must leave the cash point even for a moment, lock the drawer and take the key, or log off.
Too much cash in the drawer
When the drawer holds a lot of large notes, make a **safe drop**: move them to the safe with a signed record and a witness, as the property says.
Do not count large amounts in front of guests. Keep notes out of sight.
Do not let anyone else use your drawer or your login. Keep your own money and bag away from the drawer.
Check notes; keep cards in sight; never write PINs or card numbers.
Guests' names, room numbers and card details are private. Do not say them aloud or leave bills where others can read them.

blocks.h: If someone threatens you and demands the cash

ul: **Stay calm. Do as they say. Do not fight back or try to be a hero.** Money can be replaced; you cannot.
Give them what they ask for, quietly and slowly, without sudden movements.
Try to remember what they look like: height, clothes, voice, anything unusual, and which way they went.
Do not chase them.

blocks.p: **After they have gone:** make sure everyone is safe, lock the doors if you can do so safely, call the police and your supervisor, do not touch anything the person touched, write down what you remember, and wait for instructions. Do not discuss it with guests; refer them to the manager.

blocks.note: Your property will have a robbery procedure and may have a silent alarm. Learn it on your first day. The aim is that nobody is hurt.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Follow the property's rules on tips. Do not accept money from a guest in place of a proper payment. Do not give guests 'special' prices unless a manager has approved it. Do not take part in 'sweethearting' (giving friends free or cheap items).

At the end of a shift you **cash up**: count what is in the drawer, compare it with what the POS says should be there, and record any difference. **Reconciling** means matching what you counted with what the records say, for each type of payment.

flow: Close the drawer to new sales; print the shift report from the POS
Take the drawer to a quiet, secure place
Count all the cash, note by note and coin by coin; J$ and US$ separately
Write the totals by value on the cash-up sheet
Take away the float; put it aside for the next shift. What remains is the **cash takings**
Add up the card slips (or the terminal report), room-charge slips and vouchers
Compare each total with the matching figure on the POS report
Find, record and report any difference
Seal the takings in a bag with a deposit slip, sign it, and put it in the safe or send it to the bank or office as the property says

head: Step
Figures
Result
rows: Cash sales on the POS report
What the cash takings should be

blocks.p: Check each payment type, not only cash. The POS report might show J$142,000 in total sales: cash J$68,100, card J$51,400, room charges J$18,500 and vouchers J$4,000. Your slips must add up to the same figures: card slips J$51,400, room-charge slips J$18,500 and vouchers J$4,000. If the card total differs, you may have missed a slip or keyed an amount wrongly.

head: Result
Name
What you do
rows: Counted cash is less than the report
Do not hide or fix it. Recount, check for missed voids or errors, then record it and report it to the supervisor.
Counted cash is more than the report
Report it the same way. It may mean change was not given or a sale was not rung up.

blocks.note: Never 'fix' a shortage or overage by taking money from another shift, from your own pocket or from the tips jar. This hides errors and possible theft. Record the figure honestly. A small, honest difference now and then is normal; a hidden one is not.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Fill in the cash-up sheet **neatly and fully**, and sign it. It is a record that can be checked later, by the supervisor, the accountant or an auditor.
Attach the POS report, card terminal report, slips, vouchers and the void and refund log.
The deposit bag must be sealed and signed, with a deposit slip inside or attached, and the bag number recorded.
Make sure the float is secured for the next shift, and the drawer is empty, open and clean as the property says.
Log off the POS and the terminal; put away pens and keys.

work out change correctly and check it twice
check a note by feel, look and tilt, and deal with a suspect note without accusing the guest
use the property's daily exchange rate to change J$ to US$ and back, and show my working
take a card payment safely, never asking for or writing down a PIN, and handle a declined card quietly
take a phone payment and wait for the confirmation
check name and room number, get a signature and post a room charge correctly
check a voucher is valid before accepting it
explain GCT and service charge, and deal calmly with a bill the guest queries
explain why voids and refunds need approval and a record

seal and sign a deposit bag and complete the cash-up sheet

The cash left after the float is taken away at cash-up.
Point of sale: the till system that records sales.
The machine that reads debit and credit cards.
The small gold or silver square on a bank card that the terminal reads.

Paying by holding a card or phone near the terminal.
The code from the bank that shows a card payment was approved.
A card payment the bank did not approve.
A fake note or coin made to look real.
The code for the Jamaican dollar.
How many J$ equal one US$; set by the property for the day.
General Consumption Tax; a tax on sales charged at the current rate.

A guest's account listing all their charges at a hotel or villa.
A bill added to the guest's room account.

The paper proof that a guest has paid.
Cancelling an item or sale on the POS before the guest pays.
Moving large notes from the drawer to the safe, with a signed record.
Counting the drawer at the end of a shift and comparing it with the POS report.

c1.title: Opening the bar at a villa in Negril
c1.text: Trainee Dwayne opens the beach bar at a Negril villa at 8:30 a.m. The supervisor, Mrs. Lindo, hands him a sealed bag for a J$15,000 float. As they count it together, they find only J$14,800: one J$200 amount is missing. The float sheet says J$15,000. Most of the notes in the bag are J$1,000 and J$5,000, with very few J$50 and J$100 notes. Mrs. Lindo is called away to answer the phone.

c2.title: A US dollar payment at the front desk in Montego Bay
c2.text: At the front desk of a Montego Bay guest house, the property's rate for the day is J$155 = US$1. Mr. Hall, a visitor from Atlanta, has a bar and restaurant bill of J$9,300. He says his bank app gave him J$160 = US$1 this morning, and he wants to pay with a US$100 note, with change in J$. Trainee Camille notices a small tear at one edge of the note.

c3.title: Card and phone payments at a restaurant in Ocho Rios
c3.text: Trainee cashier Rushane works in a restaurant in Ocho Rios. A guest, Mrs. Ellis, taps her card and the terminal shows 'Declined'. A second guest, Mr. Grant, asks Rushane to key in his PIN for him because he has forgotten his glasses. A third guest says he has paid by a phone payment app that the restaurant accepts, but Rushane cannot yet see the payment on his screen. A fourth guest leaves her card on the counter when she walks away to the washroom.

c4.title: Room charges and vouchers at a resort in Runaway Bay
c4.text: At the pool bar of a Runaway Bay resort, a guest says she is Ms. Reid in room 12 and wants to charge her bill of J$4,800 to her room. The POS shows a Ms. Reid in room 21 and a Mr. Reid in room 12. Another guest hands over a voucher from a tour company for a free dinner, but the voucher is dated three weeks ago. A day visitor, not staying at the resort, asks to put her drinks 'on my friend's room'.

c5.title: Cashing up after a Saturday shift in Mandeville
c5.text: Trainee Nordia closes her cash point at a lodge in Mandeville. The float is J$25,000. She counts J$93,600 in the drawer. The POS report shows cash sales of J$69,150, card sales of J$48,200 and room charges of J$22,300. Her card slips add up to J$48,200 and her room-charge slips to J$22,300. She cannot account for the cash difference. She is tempted to take J$550 from her own purse to make it balance.

c6.title: Problems at a front desk in Kingston
c6.text: At the front desk of a Kingston guest house, trainee Orane makes a mistake and keys in a J$6,400 charge instead of J$4,600 for a guest's lunch. The guest has not yet paid. Later, an arguing guest says his bill should be lower. Late in the evening, a man walks in, shows a knife and demands the cash from the drawer. Orane is alone at the desk.

questions.q: The float count is J$200 short of the float sheet. What should Dwayne do?
o: Sign the sheet and put in the missing J$200 from his own pocket
Tell Mrs. Lindo, and sign only when it is corrected or recorded
Sign for J$15,000 now and report any shortage later in the day
Cross out J$15,000 on the sheet and write J$14,800 in himself
questions.why: The float is signed for only when the count is right. A difference must be reported to the supervisor at once and corrected or recorded, so that Dwayne is not blamed for missing money later.

questions.q: Mrs. Lindo is called away before the float is signed. What should Dwayne do?
o: Open for service and sort it out when she comes back
Take the bag to the bar and count it in front of the guests
Wait for her, as the float is counted and signed together
Sign her name for her, so that the bar can open on time
questions.why: The float is counted and signed with the supervisor so that both are protected. Opening before it is signed means any later difference cannot be traced, and signing for someone else is dishonest.

questions.q: What is the problem with the mix of notes in this float?
o: It holds too few small notes to give change to early guests
It has too many coins, which are heavy and slow to count
It holds too much money for a small beach bar to be safe
It gives the supervisor too little control of the bar's cash
questions.why: A float must have plenty of small notes and coins so you can give change to the first guests. With mostly J$1,000 and J$5,000 notes, the first guest to pay with a large note could not be given change.

questions.q: Which rate should Camille use for Mr. Hall's payment?
o: J$160, because the guest's bank app is always the most up to date
J$155, the property's rate for the day, which she tells him
A rate halfway between the two, so that it is fair to both sides
Whichever rate the guest finds the easiest one to work with
questions.why: Only the property's rate for the day is used, because it is the rate the property has set and its records are based on it. A guest's app rate is not accepted, but Camille should tell him the rate and show her working.

questions.q: Using J$155 = US$1, how much is the J$9,300 bill in US dollars?
o: US$55
US$65
US$60
US$50
questions.why: To change J$ into US$, divide by the rate: 9,300 divided by 155 equals 60. To check, multiply back: 60 x 155 = 9,300.

questions.q: Mr. Hall gives US$100. What change in J$ should Camille give, if the policy is to give change in J$?
questions.why: US$100 less the US$60 bill leaves US$40 change. US$40 x 155 = J$6,200. Change in the other currency is worked out from the rate, not by taking off J$ and US$ numbers.

questions.q: What should Camille do about the small tear in the US$ note?
o: Refuse to look at the note, as US dollars are never accepted at a cash point
Ignore the tear, as a small tear does not change the value of a note
Accept it, and let the supervisor decide what to do at cash-up
Check it is genuine and follow the property's rule on damaged notes
questions.why: Foreign notes are checked like J$ notes, and a damaged note may be refused under the property's rules. Camille should not decide to accept it on her own and leave the loss until cash-up.

questions.q: Mrs. Ellis's card shows 'Declined'. What should Rushane do first?
o: Tell her quietly and offer to try again or another way to pay
Say loudly that her card is not good so that the queue can move on
Ask her to tell him her PIN so that he can key it in himself
Keep her card at the desk until she brings enough cash to pay
questions.why: A declined card is handled quietly and politely, and the guest is offered another way to pay. Never ask for a PIN, keep a guest's card or discuss the problem where others can hear.

questions.q: Mr. Grant asks Rushane to key in his PIN. What is the right response?
o: Look away and key it in, as the guest has asked for help
Ask him to say the number out loud, so he can check it
Politely hand him the terminal so he keys in his own PIN
Write the PIN on a slip so that the guest cannot forget it
questions.why: Only the cardholder should know and key in the PIN. A cashier who handles PINs could be blamed for later fraud. If Mr. Grant cannot see the terminal, another payment method may be better.

questions.q: The guest says he has paid by phone, but Rushane cannot see it on his screen. What should Rushane do?
o: Let him go, and look for the payment later in the evening
Ask him politely to wait until the confirmation shows on screen
Accept his word, as most guests are honest about their phone payments
Ask him to pay again and claim the first payment back later on
questions.why: A phone payment is only complete when the confirmation shows. Without it, the property may not have been paid. Rushane can ask politely and check, without accusing the guest.

questions.q: The guest says she is Ms. Reid in room 12, but the POS shows a Ms. Reid in room 21. What should the bar attendant do?
o: Charge it to room 12, as she gave that room number herself
Charge it to room 21, as the name matches the record on screen
Charge it to either room and sort it out later at check-out
Check her key card or ID and confirm with the front desk
questions.why: Name and room number must match the records before a charge is posted. A wrong charge lands on another guest's folio. Check her key card or ID and ask the front desk to confirm.

questions.q: The tour company voucher is three weeks old. What should the attendant do first?
o: Accept it, as the guest cannot be blamed for the date on the voucher
Check whether it has expired, and call the supervisor if unsure
Tear it up, to prevent anyone else from using it again later
Keep the voucher and give the guest a free dinner anyway as a gift
questions.why: A voucher must be valid and for this property. If the date has passed or the attendant is unsure, the supervisor decides. Accepting or tearing up the voucher is not the attendant's choice.

questions.q: The day visitor asks to put her drinks on a friend's room. What should the attendant say?
o: Yes, as long as she can say the friend's name and room correctly
Yes, if the friend's room has been paid for in advance
No, but she may pay another way, or the friend can sign the bill
No, and she must leave the bar straight away without a drink
questions.why: Only the guest in the room, or someone with that guest's agreement, can charge to it, and the guest should sign. Offer another way to pay or ask the friend to confirm. There is no need to make a scene.

questions.q: What are Nordia's cash takings for the shift?
questions.why: Cash takings are the cash counted less the float: 93,600 - 25,000 = 68,600.

questions.q: How does Nordia's count compare with the POS cash sales of J$69,150?
o: There is an overage of J$550
The count balances exactly
There is a shortage of J$550
There is a shortage of J$1,550
questions.why: Cash takings of J$68,600 are J$550 less than the J$69,150 the POS expects, so the drawer is J$550 short.

questions.q: Nordia's card and room-charge slips match the POS. What should she do about the J$550 shortage?
o: Put in J$550 of her own money so that the drawer balances
Take J$550 from the next shift's float to make up the difference
Record the shortage honestly and report it to the supervisor
Round the count up and say nothing, as it is a small amount
questions.why: A shortage is recorded and reported, never hidden by moving money. Using her own money or another shift's money hides the error and possible theft, and it is not allowed.

questions.q: How should Nordia deal with the takings after cashing up?
o: Put them in an envelope and leave it in the drawer overnight, locked
Hand them to a colleague who is going home, to bring in the next day
Take them home with her and bring them back the next morning
Seal and sign them in a bag with a deposit slip for the safe
questions.why: Takings are sealed, signed and recorded in a bag with a deposit slip, then placed in the safe or sent to the bank or office as the property says. Anything else leaves the money unprotected.

questions.q: Orane keyed in J$6,400 instead of J$4,600 and the guest has not paid. What should Orane do?
o: Tell the supervisor, who approves a void or correction
Carry on, and give the guest J$1,800 back from the drawer later on
Change the amount on the POS without telling anybody else about it
Collect the J$6,400 from the guest and keep the difference for the shift
questions.why: A mistake before payment is corrected by a void or correction that the supervisor approves, with a record. Changing it silently or keeping the difference would look like theft.

questions.q: The guest says his bill should be lower. What should Orane do first?
o: Give him a discount to avoid an argument
Listen, then go through the bill with him, item by item
Tell him the POS is never wrong
Ask him to pay now and complain to the manager afterwards
questions.why: Listen, then check the bill with him, item by item. If there is a real mistake, the supervisor approves a correction. A discount without authority, or refusing to look, makes the problem worse.

questions.q: A man with a knife demands the cash. What is the safest thing for Orane to do?
o: Press the alarm and shout for help from the other staff at once
Try to take the knife away, as the man is alone and she is nearby
Stay calm, hand over the cash and remember what he looks like
Lock the drawer and refuse to open it for him, whatever he says
questions.why: Staff safety comes before money. Stay calm, do as asked, do not fight, and remember details of the person. Afterwards, call the police and the supervisor, and follow the property's procedure.
